# input: # No space between the number and the unit, on input or output, and no number
# agreement of any kind: 1 and 5 take the same word.
# The particles are bound morphemes, welded to the noun in front of them. After
# a Latin alias the boundary is visible and 를 lexes as a token of its own, so
# the conversion above parses with or without the space. After a Hangul unit it
# does not: "2메가비트를 비트" has no boundary to lex at and is rejected — the
# consequence `@smartput/core/locale/ko` records. A *bare* quantity is fine
# either way, because `particleStripper` peels the ending off the unit word.
# The myriad. Korean counts in ten-thousands, so 만 is a magnitude word in its
# own right and 일만 is one of them, not ten of a thousand. The separators
# printed are English's — "," for groups, and the "." in the "0.25Gbps" above.
# The Hangul transcriptions of the borrowed nouns. "메가비트" and "메가바이트"
# name two kinds, and the factor of 8 between them is the one the bridge
# The word operators need whitespace around them even though Korean glues its
# particles: "2mbps곱하기3" does not parse. The symbol operators above have no
# such requirement, and neither do the particles.
